title: Introduce BitCast (reinterpret cast)
body:
# New Operator

## Describe the operator

- Following https://github.com/onnx/onnx/issues/4343, the only operator missing is BitCast. With models coming from frameworks often do reinterpretation of weights (https://github.com/onnx/onnx/issues/4343#issuecomment-2753441860, https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/126921). A simple example is

```py
class Float4Module(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, input: torch.Tensor):
        input = input.view(torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2)
        return input
```

### Implementation cost

Being a fundamental operator in programming languages and hardwares, supporting the operator should be straightfoward.

## Can this operator be constructed using existing onnx operators?

No.

## Is this operator used by any model currently? Which one?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
`BitCast` would be useful for Chromium when the underlying backend awkwardly missed registering some data types, notably for pure data movement operators (gather/scatter/where/onehot/tile...) where the data type representation doesn't matter anyway. One example is the `where` operator where ORT's CPU EP supports `uint8` and `int32`, but surprisingly *not* `int8` and `uint32` (even though it would introduce no additional DLL code bloat to support both uint8 and int8, since they are bitwise identical). With `BitCast`, at least the caller (Chromium) could mitigate the issue and insert a BitCast before reaching ORT (and then remove it if ORT handles the data types directly). Context: - "ORT CPU EP should support int8, uint32, and uint64 for where operation"
https:///issues/429859156 - "WebNN: Implement where operation for ORT backend"
https:///c/chromium/src/+/6702792 - "add minimum data types and rank range for operations"
https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webnn/pull/910

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant1 assigned to copilot. What should the behavior be when dtype bit widths are different?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Looks like this is tf's behavior:

If the input datatype T is larger than the output datatype type then the shape changes from [...] to [..., sizeof(T)/sizeof(type)].

If T is smaller than type, the operator requires that the rightmost dimension be equal to sizeof(type)/sizeof(T). The shape then goes from [..., sizeof(type)/sizeof(T)] to [...].

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> What should the behavior be when dtype bit widths are different?
> Looks like this is tf's behavior

@reporter: Hmm, that's novel. I've only ever needed bit casting between elements of the *same size*, and casting between elements of differing bitsizes introduces a few important other questions:

- What happens for elements that are not multiples of each other? e.g. uint32 input and [float6](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7145) output
- What about endianness issues? Although ONNX *files* store their data in LE, I could see a BE device loading the model and byte-swapping the data, such that during *execution*, the data is BE. So then you have some awkward splicing if you bitcast a uint32 to 2x uint16's, because the uint16's would exchange even/odd coordinates depending on architecture.

So I feel safer *starting out* with the restriction that `bitsizeof(input.dataType) == bitsizeof(output.dataType)`, and then relaxing it later upon encountering TF models (converted to ONNX) that do such mixing, plus clearly documenting the expectations of such cases (saying it is "implementation defined" wouldn't be so good for predictable interchange). TF might be able to make some LE assumptions (like, maybe TF only builds to x86/x64/arm architectures 🤷‍♂️), and ORT only targets LE machines too (that I've *seen*), but ONNX as an interchange IR isn't necessary limited to one architecture.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Makes sense to me! @participant4 do you have thoughts?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Does it mean there is no way then to re-interpret anything to a float6 dtype?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant3 would you like to chime in? I remember you needed to reinterpret uint32 to float8 or something?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: > Does it mean there is no way then to re-interpret anything to a float6 dtype? Well, if a future `float3` or `float12` exists, then that would be a nice multiple of `float6` 😉. Actually, if you had a byte array of `uint8[3,4,6]`, that reasonably could be castable to `float6[3,4,8]` (or `uint8[3,4,3]` and `float6[3,4,4]`), because the last dimension has the same number of bits wide for the lowest dimension stride:      So I'm not *opposed* to reinterpreting across different element bit sizes (certainly there could be some perf benefits to a reinterpret cast to a larger type if you wanted to perform an operation in parallel), but if we do, we need to document these cases clearly (how it affects the last dimension, compatibility constraints, and endianness clarity).

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: How about we say that the output will just be a **1d tensor**, and the user will reshape it afterward?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> How about we say that the output will just be a **1d tensor**, and the user will reshape it afterward?

You mean that for cases where the element bit sizes are identical (e.g. uint32 and float32, uint8 and bool8...), directly accept ND shapes (without requiring the caller to reshape to 1D first then back to the original shape again), but for cases of incompatible element bit sizes, require the input/output to be 1D? That's one way to avoid deciding policy around the oddly shaped cases, and I'm okay with that. I'd require the *input* to be 1D too though for such cases, as it would be weirdly asymmetric to accept any *input* ND shape but only *output* a 1D tensor. Also, we still expect the *total tensor* bit counts to be compatible in either case (e.g. total bit size `uint8[3,4,3]` matches that of `float6[3,4,4]`, because otherwise we'd have to trim down the leftover bits to match),

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: @reporter : my use case was to reinterpret floating data type as same-size integer data type (to avoid automatic conversion of a buffer by model.float() etc). I did find a workaround later, but I do believe supporting direct translation of view(dtype) is important for coverage. Yes I am OK with requiring  1D shape on input/output in cases where sizes are not the same.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
After reviewing [the PR](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7527) and considering the cases, I am more comfortable with allowing differing element bit sizes between input and output (given the last dimension has the same total bit count) without needing to go between 1D first and back.

I left a comment about endianness to clarify that implementations should execute *as if* the data was little endian (because the ONNX file is already baked with LE weights, and so the model expects certain results), which means more work for any BE ONNX implementations (as they'd have to byteswap the elements, if there even are any implementations of ONNX on BE hardware), but it's no extra work for LE implementations (each EP just reinterprets the tensor data). Note any hypothetical BE implementations *already* have to behave *as if* little endian anyway for UINT4 and UINT2 element types.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Comment from today's sig-operators meeting: we will support dtypes of only the same bitwidth.
